title: Deception in Mass Autonomous Warfare
gist: Édouard Maurin, a veteran of the Pokrovsk fighting, argues deception must be redesigned for a sensor-saturated battlefield: target the automated sensing-classification-decision chain, nest signature management across echelons, and judge decoys by economic and operational profitability, citing Russian decoy drones and Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi.

insights.claim: On a battlefield made transparent by sensors, concealment alone no longer protects maneuver, so deception should target the whole automated chain of sensing, fusion, classification and decision, not only the enemy commander.
insights.speaker: Édouard R. Maurin
insights.so_what: Demand for decoys, spoofing and signature-management products grows as the battlefield becomes machine-read.

insights.claim: Maurin's fake radio call at Kotlyne in January 2025 drew two Russian soldiers out within two minutes, showing deception can serve as reconnaissance, provoke a visible response, and divert attention.
insights.speaker: Édouard R. Maurin
insights.so_what: Illustrates the cheap sense-test-iterate loop that machine-speed deception enables.

insights.claim: Since 2024 Russian strike packages have used foam Gerbera and wooden Parodiya decoy drones with Luneburg lenses, reportedly 50 percent of swarms, priced under $10,000 each versus Western interceptors costing hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars.
insights.speaker: Édouard R. Maurin
insights.so_what: Cost exchange ratios favor decoy spam, which drives demand for cheap interceptors.

insights.claim: Ukraine responded with cheaper interceptors such as the $2,500 Sting drone from Wild Hornets and its own long-range decoy Spectr from OM Defence System.
insights.speaker: Édouard R. Maurin
insights.so_what: Low-cost interceptor and decoy makers benefit from this exchange-ratio logic.

insights.claim: FPV drones with thermal cameras cost about $2,500 in 2024 but mass production now puts them at roughly $400 per unit excluding sensor and payload, so ground decoys aimed at them must cost a fraction of that to be economical.
insights.speaker: Édouard R. Maurin
insights.so_what: FPV cost collapse makes expensive inflatable decoys uneconomic against drones.
insights.locator: First-person view drone with a thermal camera

insights.claim: Maurin defines profitability as whether the adversary spends more than the deceiver to engage a decoy and whether the deception buys freedom of action; a costlier decoy can still pay if it opens a corridor or saturates classifiers.
insights.speaker: Édouard R. Maurin
insights.so_what: A usable lens for evaluating decoy and EW procurement.
insights.locator: Even if a ground decoy exceeds the cost

insights.claim: In Operation Vivaldi in September 2026, Ukraine's Third Army Corps under Andriy Biletsky used electronic warfare, information silence and fabricated battlefield pictures to retake Nove; deputy commander Maksym Zhorin said a protective EW dome helped disrupt around 20,000 Russian drones.
insights.speaker: Édouard R. Maurin
insights.so_what: Evidence that integrated EW and deception are restoring maneuver for Ukraine.

insights.claim: Maurin notes the effect on automated classifiers is his proposal, not an observed result, and that decoy effectiveness windows are likely short as adversaries retrain.
insights.speaker: Édouard R. Maurin
insights.so_what: Treat classifier-spoofing as unproven; it is an adaptation race.

insights.claim: Existing doctrine such as JP 3-13.4 presumes a human decision-maker; the author proposes nesting signature management across echelons into one consistent story, with a battalion-level signature management cell holding the library and reprogramming emitters.
insights.speaker: Édouard R. Maurin
insights.so_what: Points to demand for emitters, reprogrammable decoys and spectrum-management tooling.

insights.claim: The advantage of a decoy persists only while the deceiver's variation period is shorter than the defender's adaptation cycle, and digitally reprogrammable emitters can change parameters faster than a defender can collect, label and retrain.
insights.speaker: Édouard R. Maurin
insights.so_what: Software-defined, rapidly updatable decoys have the edge over fixed hardware.

insights.claim: Western armies have cut deception and electronic warfare specialists to very little over three decades, and reintroducing the capability requires reallocation or new capacity; acquisition authorities should issue calls for proximity camouflage and low-cost active decoy solutions fieldable at scale.
insights.speaker: Édouard R. Maurin
insights.so_what: Signals a potential procurement opening for EW and decoy startups.
